title: Love to be unknown (I.2)
hook: every post asks to be seen; chapter two of the Imitation says love to be unknown, and ties it to learning
tomorrow: what can one afternoon teach you that no book can?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd stung to the heart, and a book that would rather feel compunction than define it. The line was feel, not define.

Views. Likes. Seen by. Almost everything on a phone counts who noticed. So here's a strange line from chapter two of The Imitation of Christ. If you want to know and learn something worth having, it says, love to be unknown. Not put up with being unknown. Love it. And the odd part is where it puts the line: in a chapter about learning. Why would being unnoticed help anyone learn?
screen: `VIEWS. LIKES. SEEN BY.` → `LOVE TO BE UNKNOWN.` → `WHY WOULD THAT HELP YOU LEARN?`

segments.voice: Follow the chapter and the puzzle starts to open. It begins by saying people naturally want to know things. Fine. But a humble farmhand who serves God, it says, is better than a proud philosopher who studies the course of the stars and neglects himself. The more you know, the more you'll answer for, unless your life is better for it. Then the turn: know yourself, humbly. And the Latin for the line that follows is two words: ama nesciri. Love to be unknown. Here's one way to read why it belongs here. When you need to be seen as someone who knows, every new lesson becomes a threat to the image, and you stop learning to protect it. A person who doesn't need the audience can say I was wrong, I don't know, teach me. Being unknown frees you to stay a beginner. Jesus says something close in Matthew's Gospel about giving. In the Douay-Rheims: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Give quietly, he says, and the Father who sees in secret will repay. The thing to tell a friend tonight: a whole chapter on learning turns on two Latin words, love to be unknown.
screen: `THE FARMHAND AND THE STARGAZER.` · `KNOW YOURSELF, HUMBLY.` · `AMA NESCIRI: LOVE TO BE UNKNOWN.` · `NO AUDIENCE, STILL LEARNING.` · then, large: `UNKNOWN.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing you could do tomorrow that no one will ever see: refill something, fix something, pray for someone by name. Notice the small itch to mention it later. Decide now that when the itch comes, you'll smile and let it pass.
Love to be unknown. Chapter two's counsel: do good and keep learning, free of needing anyone to notice.
Your line: unknown. The left hand doesn't need to hear what the right hand did. Good night.

fork.setup: your parish posts a thank-you list for its food drive. a friend asks to be left off it, and someone calls that fake modesty. what would chapter two say?
options: she's loving to be unknown: doing good without needing the praise.
she should be listed, since being seen is the real point of giving.
she's hiding because she must be ashamed of how little she gave.
fork.reveal: the Imitation's ama nesciri and Jesus's left hand and right hand point the same way: the good is done for God, who sees in secret.

chat.says: made mia a late birthday playlist. took four hours. should i tell her how long it took?
options: Let that part stay unknown. The gift is the gift; the hours don't need an audience.
Yes. If she knows the effort, she'll see you're sorry, and that's what matters.
Don't give it at all. A gift she knows about can't really be humble.
chat.meaning: Chapter two says love to be unknown, and Jesus says let not the left hand know what the right hand does. The good doesn't need an audience.
